subject: Pathology
summary: Valvular heart disease (VHD) is structural damage to heart valves causing stenosis or regurgitation, leading to pressure or volume overload and heart failure if untreated.

sections.p: VHD refers to any abnormality of valve leaflets, annulus, or supporting structures that impairs forward flow (stenosis) or causes backward flow (regurgitation). Diagnosis relies on clinical exam and imaging.
b: Murmur characteristics (timing, location, radiation) guide suspicion
Echocardiography confirms valve anatomy, severity, and hemodynamics

t.b: What murmur pattern is present? A systolic ejection murmur suggests stenosis; a holosystolic murmur suggests regurgitation.
What is valve area, gradient, and regurgitant volume? Confirms severity and guides management.

sections.p: Severity is graded by valve area, pressure gradient (stenosis) or regurgitant fraction (regurgitation) per ESC guidelines.
b: Aortic stenosis: mild >1.5 cm², moderate 1.0–1.5 cm², severe <1.0 cm²
Mitral regurgitation: mild <30%, moderate 30‑49%, severe ≥50%

sections.p: Causes differ by valve and region; consider epidemiology and patient age.
b: Rheumatic fever – most common cause of mitral stenosis worldwide
Degenerative calcification – leading cause of aortic stenosis in older adults
Congenital bicuspid aortic valve – early calcific disease
Infective endocarditis – acute regurgitation, common with HIV, IV drug use
Post‑radiation or connective‑tissue disease (e.g., Marfan)

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the type of overload and the valve involved.
b: Stenosis: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope (triad)
Regurgitation: fatigue, palpitations, pulmonary edema (left side) or peripheral edema (right side)

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: What is cardiac size and pulmonary congestion? Enlarged silhouette suggests chronic volume overload; normal size does not exclude severe disease.
What rhythm or chamber strain is present? Atrial fibrillation often accompanies mitral disease; LV hypertrophy suggests aortic stenosis.

t.a: Transesophageal echo (if TTE unavailable or inconclusive)
t.b: What detailed valve anatomy is needed? Provides superior view of prosthetic valves and vegetations.
What is ventricular function when echo windows are poor? Quantifies regurgitant volume and fibrosis.

sections.p: Identify features that signal imminent decompensation.
b: Sudden worsening dyspnea or orthopnea
New onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Syncope or presyncope in stenosis
Signs of endocarditis: fever, new murmur, embolic phenomena

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve overload, and prevent progression.
b: Rheumatic disease: secondary prophylaxis with penicillin to prevent recurrence
Infective endocarditis: IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + vancomycin) after cultures
Heart failure: diuretics for congestion, ACE‑inhibitors/ARNI for remodeling, beta‑blockers for rate control
Severe stenosis or regurgitation: valve repair or replacement (surgical or transcatheter) when symptoms or ventricular dysfunction develop
Echo every 1–2 years for mild/moderate disease, sooner if symptoms change
Blood pressure control and lipid management reduce progression
Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal) to avoid decompensation

sections.p: Conditions that mimic valve murmurs or symptoms.
b: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy – systolic ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva
Pulmonary hypertension – can produce a tricuspid regurgitation murmur
Anemia – high‑output state causing flow murmurs
Mild regurgitation on echo may be underestimated in tachycardia
Normal gradient in severe aortic stenosis if low cardiac output
Absence of fever does not rule out subacute endocarditis

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain, syncope, severe shortness of breath, new rapid heart rhythm, fever with a new murmur

faq.q: Why does rheumatic fever mainly affect the mitral valve?
faq.a: Molecular mimicry targets the mitral valve’s connective tissue, leading to chronic inflammation and scarring.

faq.q: Can a patient with mild aortic stenosis be asymptomatic?
faq.a: Yes; many remain symptom‑free until the valve area falls below 1.0 cm² or ventricular function declines.
No; transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is an option for high‑risk patients with severe aortic stenosis.

exam: Describe how you would differentiate aortic stenosis from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on physical exam and echo.
List the ESC criteria for severe mitral regurgitation and explain why surgery is indicated at that stage.
Explain the role of secondary penicillin prophylaxis in preventing progression of rheumatic mitral disease.
